articles.title: India's Tiger Population Reaches 3,682 — A 200% Recovery in Four Decades
articles.excerpt: India's latest tiger census confirms the national population has reached 3,682 individuals — the highest recorded count in the country's conservation history and a landmark in Project Tiger's 50-year trajectory.
articles.summary: India's 2024 tiger census confirms a national population of 3,682 individuals across 54 tiger reserves and surrounding landscapes. This represents a 6.7% increase from the 2022 count and validates four decades of landscape-level conservation investment.
articles.whyItMatters: India is home to 75% of the world's wild tigers. This recovery demonstrates that science-led, community-supported conservation at landscape scale can reverse species decline — a model with global implications.

articles.title: Vulture Restaurants Bring Critically Endangered Species Back from the Edge
articles.excerpt: Supplementary feeding stations — known as vulture restaurants — have contributed to a measurable population increase in three critically endangered Gyps species across northern India, with breeding pairs recorded at seven new sites in 2024.
articles.summary: Wildlife Trust of India's vulture restaurant network, now spanning 18 sites across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttar Pradesh, has supported a 23% increase in Gyps vulture sightings at monitored locations. Seven new breeding pairs were confirmed in 2024 — the first natural colonisation events in the region in over a decade.
articles.whyItMatters: India's vulture collapse in the 1990s — caused by veterinary diclofenac — was one of the fastest species declines ever recorded. These breeding confirmations represent a genuine turning point in what seemed an irreversible trajectory.

articles.title: Lakshadweep Coral Bleaching Resilience Study Identifies Survivor Colonies
articles.source: National Centre for Sustainable Coastal Management
articles.excerpt: A five-year resilience study in Lakshadweep has identified 34 coral colonies that survived three bleaching events without mortality — providing genetic material for reef restoration and heat-tolerance research.
articles.summary: Researchers from NCSCM identified 34 thermally resistant coral colonies across Lakshadweep's atolls that survived three bleaching events between 2019 and 2024 with zero mortality. These colonies, spanning 7 genera, are now the foundation of a reef restoration programme aimed at propagating heat-tolerant coral across bleaching-vulnerable sites.
articles.whyItMatters: Heat-tolerant coral genetics represent one of the most tangible tools for reef futures under climate warming. These survivor colonies are both a scientific resource and a reason for measured hope in tropical marine conservation.

articles.title: Community Forest Rights Act Protects 2.7 Million Hectares of Tribal Forest Land
articles.excerpt: Implementation of Community Forest Rights under the Forest Rights Act has now formally recognised 2.7 million hectares of tribal forest land across 12 states — a legal milestone that simultaneously protects biodiversity and secures indigenous livelihoods.
articles.summary: A new assessment confirms that Community Forest Rights recognition under India's Forest Rights Act now covers 2.7 million hectares across 12 states, granting 1.2 million tribal households formal governance rights over forests they have managed for generations. Studies show that community-governed forests have 40% lower deforestation rates than state-managed equivalents.
articles.whyItMatters: The most effective forest protection often comes not from exclusion but from recognition. Formal rights give communities both the legal standing and the incentive to defend landscapes that conventional conservation cannot reach.

articles.title: India's Gangetic Dolphin Population Shows Recovery in Cleaned River Reaches
articles.excerpt: Population surveys along stretches of the Ganga where industrial effluent has been controlled show a 34% increase in Gangetic dolphin sightings over five years — a response linked to measurable improvements in river water quality.
articles.summary: WWF India's 2024 Gangetic dolphin survey documents a 34% sighting increase in river reaches where Namami Gange pollution interventions have improved water quality. The survey covered 1,200 kilometres of river across Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, recording 854 individual dolphins — the highest count in the monitored stretches in 15 years.
articles.whyItMatters: Gangetic dolphins are the Ganga's primary ecological indicator species. Their recovery in cleaned reaches is direct, measurable evidence that river restoration works — and a powerful argument for expanding pollution control across the basin.

articles.title: Rewilding in Rajasthan: Cheetahs Adapt to Kuno After Two Years
articles.excerpt: Two years after their reintroduction at Kuno National Park, behavioural studies confirm that three adult cheetahs have established consistent home ranges, made independent kills, and show signs of adaptation to Indian prey dynamics.
articles.summary: Behavioural monitoring of the Kuno cheetah population confirms that three adult individuals have established stable home ranges averaging 47 square kilometres, made independent kills of chital and nilgai, and reduced their reliance on supplementary feeding. One adult female is under health monitoring but the wider programme shows promising adaptation signals.
articles.whyItMatters: The cheetah reintroduction is the most closely watched rewilding experiment in Indian conservation history. Evidence of independent establishment, however early, suggests that ecological restoration at species level is achievable in the subcontinent.
